stories.text: John Leavers lived here, at Canning Circus, where a plaque calls him the inventor of the Leavers lace machine, in 1813. He improved John Heathcoat's lace machine, and in 1821 emigrated to Grand-Couronne in Normandy.
Building began in 1841 on a Catholic church designed by Augustus Pugin, with much of the cost paid by Lord Shrewsbury. It was consecrated in 1844, and in 1852 it became a cathedral.
Augustus Pugin, who also designed the interior of the Houses of Parliament, designed the cathedral.[^s1][^s2]

73761.sum: The Cathedral Church of St. Barnabas is a cathedral of the Roman Catholic Church in the city of Nottingham in Nottinghamshire, England. It is the mother church of the Diocese of Nottingham and seat of the Bishop of Nottingham.

stories.text: A legacy from the banker John Key paid for a hospital on part of Nottingham Park. Its first building, designed by John Simpson, was begun on 12 February 1781 and opened with 44 beds in September 1782; John Wesley was an early visitor. In 1844 it took in the hurt from a hanging on High Pavement, where twelve died on Garner's Hill: Wikipedia says a stand collapsed, but the newspapers of the day describe the crowd being forced down the steps into Garner's Hill and trampled.[^crush] Hine added a storey in 1855, and Alfred Waterhouse's round Jubilee Wing opened in 1900. It closed in 1992, its work moved to the Queen's Medical Centre.

73960.sum: Nottingham General Hospital was a major hospital in Nottingham, England. It was founded in 1781 and closed in 1992.

73961.sum: The Roundhouse Bar and Kitchen is a pub on Royal Standard Place. The building was built in 1897, according to OpenStreetMap. It was designed by Alfred Waterhouse.

stories.text: Built in 1887–88 to designs by Thomas Verity and George Henry Hunt, chosen in a competition judged by Alfred Waterhouse, it replaced the old Guild Hall on Weekday Cross and served as the city's magistrates' court. The council used it as offices until 2010; it has stood largely empty since.

74995.sum: Nottingham Guildhall is a former magistrates' court in Nottingham, England. The structure, which was used by Nottingham City Council as offices in the 1990s, is a Grade II listed building.

stories.text: Nottingham Victoria, the Great Central and Great Northern railways' station, opened on 24 May 1900 and closed on 4 September 1967. It was demolished except for its clock tower, which still stands at the entrance of the Victoria Centre built on the site.

75086.sum: Nottingham Victoria station: a takeaway. The building was built in 1899, according to OpenStreetMap. It is Grade II listed as Victoria Centre Clock Tower and was designed by Albert Edward Lambert.

stories.text: A shopping centre opened in 1972 on the site of Nottingham Victoria railway station, whose clock tower still stands beside it.

75088.sum: Victoria Centre: a shopping centre on Victoria Centre. The building was built in 1972, according to Wikipedia.

stories.text: Building on the new School of Art in Waverley Street began on 23 May 1863, but its foundation stone waited until 22 October, when the 5th Duke of Newcastle could come. He was then the Provincial Grand Master of Nottinghamshire's Freemasons, and he laid the stone with the usual Masonic ceremonies; the band played "God Save the Queen" and the crowd joined in.[^mmr] Thirty-five years later it was remembered as the last such ceremony the Masons had performed in Nottingham itself.[^fcn]

stories.text: On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.
Built between 1877 and 1881 for University College Nottingham, where D. H. Lawrence studied during his teacher-training years.[^s1]

76264.sum: The Arkwright Building is a Grade II* listed university building on Shakespeare Street in Nottingham, England. It forms part of the Nottingham Trent University City Campus and is one of the university's principal historic buildings. Built between 1877 and 1881, the building was originally home to University College Nottingham, the city library and a natural history museum.

stories.text: For more than a century Nottingham's Freemasons had no hall of their own. One lodge, meeting in the town from 1755, moved from inn to inn: the Red Lion on Climber Street by 1763, the Leg of Mutton on Sandy Lane, then three inns on Parliament Street in turn, the Kingstone Arms, the New George and the Milton's Head, and later the Crown and Cushion, the Poultry Hotel and the Castle and Falcon on Warser Gate. From 1844 it met in the Assembly Rooms on Low Pavement, and in 1881 it settled at the Masonic Hall on Goldsmith Street.[^lane] Another lodge, named after the Milton's Head inn, whose records run from 1790, belonged to the rival Antients; its warrant was cancelled in 1799 and restored the next year.[^tna]

stories.text: When the Duke of St Albans became Nottinghamshire's Provincial Grand Master in 1878, the brethren raised the idea of a hall of their own. It was built here on Goldsmith Street and opened in 1880, as a meeting place for the lodges and a Masonic club.[^fcn] Lodges that had met in inns moved in from 1881.[^lane] The present hall, of brick with stone details in the Neo-Classical style usual for Masonic halls, was designed in 1928 by John Howitt & Son, one of the last works of John Howitt, himself a Freemason; the city lists it as a local heritage asset.[^insight] The first lodge consecrated in it was Temple Lodge, on 30 October 1930.[^temple]
